plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a single upward-opening parabola on a coordinate plane and annotates its main features with labeled arrows. Both axes are numbered from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid, with x labeled at the right end of the horizontal axis and y at the top of the vertical one. The curve is a heavy teal U with arrowheads on both rising branches; its lowest point sits at x equal to 1, y equal to -4, and the branches climb to about y equal to 5 near x equal to -2 on the left and x equal to 4 on the right. Small filled dots mark the two crossings of the x-axis at x equal to -1 and x equal to 3, the crossing of the y-axis at y equal to -3, the turning point, and the mirror partner of the y-intercept at x equal to 2. A red dashed vertical line runs through x equal to 1, reached by an arrow from the label Axis of symmetry above. Three further labels point to the graph and read x-intercepts, y-intercept, and Vertex. Drawing the dashed line through the turning point lets the reader check that the marked dots sit at equal heights on either side. The graph fixes the vocabulary for reading a quadratic.

interactionPlan.concept: A parabola's vertex sets both its turning point and its axis of symmetry, and the quadratic's stretch factor controls how far the x-intercepts sit from that axis.

Filled black dots at the x-intercepts (-1, 0) and (3, 0)

Label 'Vertex' at bottom with an arrow pointing to (1,-4)

interactions.teaches: The vertex alone determines the turning point AND the location of the axis of symmetry: move it and the dashed line, the mirror pair, and the intercepts all follow.

demo_steps.title: The labeled parabola
demo_steps.narration: The teal curve y = (x-1)^2 - 4 turns at the vertex (1, -4), crosses the x-axis at -1 and 3, and crosses the y-axis at -3. Every feature has a name.

demo_steps.title: Reading the intercepts
demo_steps.narration: Focus on the crossings only: two x-intercepts where the curve meets y = 0, and one y-intercept where it meets x = 0. These are the solutions and the starting height of the quadratic.

demo_steps.title: The mirror line
demo_steps.narration: Now emphasize symmetry. The red dashed line through the vertex reflects the curve onto itself: the y-intercept at (0,-3) has a partner at (2,-3), the same height and the same distance from x = 1.

demo_steps.title: Drag the vertex
demo_steps.narration: Drag the vertex anywhere on the plane. The dashed axis of symmetry slides to stay under it, the mirror pair stays level, and the x-intercepts move — or disappear when the vertex rises above the x-axis.

demo_steps.title: Stretch and squeeze
demo_steps.narration: Increase a and the parabola narrows, pulling the x-intercepts toward the axis of symmetry; decrease a and they spread apart. The axis itself never moves.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The vertex is the anchor of the whole graph — it fixes the minimum and the mirror line — while the coefficient a only controls how fast the curve widens, so it slides the x-intercepts toward or away from that fixed line.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Square coordinate plane, both axes -6 to 6, light gray dotted grid at integers, thin black axes with arrowheads and 'x' / 'y' labels at the right and top. Plot a heavy teal (steel-blue) upward parabola in vertex form with arrowheads on both branches, clipped near y = 5-6. Mark five small filled black dots: vertex (1,-4), x-intercepts (-1,0) and (3,0), y-intercept (0,-3), and mirror point (2,-3). Draw the axis of symmetry as a bold red dashed vertical line through the vertex. Black label text with thin curved arrows: 'Axis of symmetry' upper right pointing down to the red line, 'x-intercepts' mid right with two arrows to the two zeros, 'y-intercept' on the left pointing right to (0,-3), 'Vertex' at bottom pointing up to the turning point. When the 'Intercepts' view is active, dim the symmetry line and pulse the three intercept dots; when 'Symmetry' is active, dim the intercept labels and emphasize the red line plus a light dashed horizontal connector between (0,-3) and (2,-3). Show a live vertex-form equation readout in a corner that updates with drag and slider.

authoredContext:
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. One important feature of the graph is that it has an extreme point, called the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex represents the lowest point on the graph, or the minimum value of the quadratic function. If the parabola opens down, the vertex represents the highest point on the graph, or the maximum value. In either case, the vertex is a turning point on the graph. The graph is also symmetric with a vertical line drawn through the vertex, called the axis of symmetry. These features are illustrated in the figure.

Graph of a parabola showing where the x and y intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry are.

The y-intercept is the point at which the parabola crosses the y-axis. The x-intercepts are the points at which the parabola crosses the x-axis. If they exist, the x-intercepts represent the zeros, or roots, of the quadratic function, the values of x at which y=0.

An extra teal equation readout 'y = (x − 1)² − 4' is drawn in the top-left corner and a pale teal halo surrounds the vertex dot; neither appears in the source figure.
Minor placement drift: the 'Vertex' label/arrow sits further right and lower than in the source, and the 'x-intercepts' label is closer to the plot edge, though both still read correctly.
evaluation.notes: Structurally and conceptually an excellent reproduction of the labeled parabola (dotted grid, arrowed axes, red dashed axis of symmetry, all marked points and leader-arrow annotations) with a rich, genuinely pedagogical set of interactions; the main deductions are small label collisions at the axis ends/tick labels and a couple of added elements (equation readout, vertex halo) not in the source.

Make the top-left equation readout optional/subtler (e.g. gray small caption) so the step-0 view matches the static source more closely, and reduce or remove the teal halo on the vertex until the vertex is hovered/dragged.
